Content:
The fundamental theorem of algebra tells us that any quartic polynomial with real coefficients has precisely four roots.

Content:
Furthermore, any such polynomial can be factored as
[MATH: ax^4+bx^3+cx^2 + dx + e = a(x-x_1)(x-x_2)(x-x_3)(x-x_4),]
where [MATH: x_1, x_2, x_3,] and [MATH: x_4] are the roots of the polynomial.

Content:
As always, when counting the roots of a quartic polynomial, we need to bear in mind the following points:

Content:
- If a root has multiplicity [MATH: 2,] we count it twice.
- Likewise, if a root has multiplicity [MATH: 3] or [MATH: 4,] we count it three or four times, respectively.
- We also include any imaginary or complex roots.

Content:
Remember that in the case of imaginary or complex roots, the roots always come in complex conjugate pairs.

sections.normalized_html:
Since our quartic polynomial has roots [MATH: {x_1=0, x_2=-1},] [MATH: {x_3=2},] and [MATH: {x_4=-3},] and the coefficient of the quartic term is [MATH: {a=4},] we can write the polynomial as follows:

[MATH: a(x − x_{1})(x − x_{2})(x − x_{3})(x − x_{4})|= 4(x − 0)(x − (− 1))(x − 2)(x − (− 3)); = 4(x − 0)(x + 1)(x − 2)(x + 3)]

Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

[MATH: 4(x − 0)(x + 1)(x − 2)(x + 3)|= 4(x^{2} + x)(x^{2} + x − 6); = 4(x^{4} + x^{3} − 6x^{2} + x^{3} + x^{2} − 6x); = 4(x^{4} + 2x^{3} − 5x^{2} − 6x); = 4x^{4} + 8x^{3} − 20x^{2} − 24x.]

Therefore, [MATH: P(x) = 4x^4+8x^3-20x^2-24x.]

items.readable_text:
Content:
In this lesson, we have considered the fundamental theorem of algebra applied to quartic polynomials. However, we remind ourselves that we can apply the fundamental theorem of algebra to any polynomial with real coefficients.

Content:
Suppose that [MATH: p(x)] is a polynomial of degree [MATH: n] with real coefficients, given by

Content:
[MATH: p(x) = a_nx^n+\ldots+a_1x+a_0, \qquad a_n\neq 0.]

Content:
The fundamental theorem of algebra tells us that [MATH: p(x)] will always have precisely [MATH: n] roots.

Content:
Furthermore, [MATH: p(x)] can be factored as follows:
[MATH: p(x) = a_n(x-x_1)(x-x_2)(x-x_3)\cdots (x-x_{n})]
where [MATH: x_1, x_2, x_3,\ldots ,x_n] are the roots of the polynomial.

Content:
As with the quadratic, cubic, and quartic cases, we need to bear the following important points in mind when counting the roots of a polynomial:

Content:
- If a root has multiplicity [MATH: m,] we count that root [MATH: m] times.
- We also include any imaginary or complex roots.

Content:
And remember, complex roots always come in complex conjugate pairs.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The fundamental theorem of algebra tells us that any quartic polynomial with real coefficients has precisely four roots.

Content:
Furthermore, any such polynomial can be factored as
[MATH: ax^4+bx^3+cx^2 + dx + e = a(x-x_1)(x-x_2)(x-x_3)(x-x_4),]
where [MATH: x_1, x_2, x_3,] and [MATH: x_4] are the roots of the polynomial.

Content:
As always, when counting the roots of a quartic polynomial, we need to bear in mind the following points:

Content:
- If a root has multiplicity [MATH: 2,] we count it twice.
- Likewise, if a root has multiplicity [MATH: 3] or [MATH: 4,] we count it three or four times, respectively.
- We also include any imaginary or complex roots.

Content:
Remember that in the case of imaginary or complex roots, the roots always come in complex conjugate pairs.

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding a Quartic Polynomial Given Four Real Roots

Example Prompt:
The quartic polynomial [MATH: P(x)] has roots [MATH: x_1=0, x_2=-1,x_3=2] and [MATH: x_4=-3,] and the coefficient of the quartic term is [MATH: 4.] Find [MATH: P(x).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Since our quartic polynomial has roots [MATH: {x_1=0, x_2=-1},] [MATH: {x_3=2},] and [MATH: {x_4=-3},] and the coefficient of the quartic term is [MATH: {a=4},] we can write the polynomial as follows:

[MATH: a(x − x_{1})(x − x_{2})(x − x_{3})(x − x_{4})|= 4(x − 0)(x − (− 1))(x − 2)(x − (− 3)); = 4(x − 0)(x + 1)(x − 2)(x + 3)]

Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

[MATH: 4(x − 0)(x + 1)(x − 2)(x + 3)|= 4(x^{2} + x)(x^{2} + x − 6); = 4(x^{4} + x^{3} − 6x^{2} + x^{3} + x^{2} − 6x); = 4(x^{4} + 2x^{3} − 5x^{2} − 6x); = 4x^{4} + 8x^{3} − 20x^{2} − 24x.]

Therefore, [MATH: P(x) = 4x^4+8x^3-20x^2-24x.]

Item 8 — Tutorial: General Statement of the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra

Content:
In this lesson, we have considered the fundamental theorem of algebra applied to quartic polynomials. However, we remind ourselves that we can apply the fundamental theorem of algebra to any polynomial with real coefficients.

Content:
Suppose that [MATH: p(x)] is a polynomial of degree [MATH: n] with real coefficients, given by

Content:
[MATH: p(x) = a_nx^n+\ldots+a_1x+a_0, \qquad a_n\neq 0.]

Content:
The fundamental theorem of algebra tells us that [MATH: p(x)] will always have precisely [MATH: n] roots.

Content:
Furthermore, [MATH: p(x)] can be factored as follows:
[MATH: p(x) = a_n(x-x_1)(x-x_2)(x-x_3)\cdots (x-x_{n})]
where [MATH: x_1, x_2, x_3,\ldots ,x_n] are the roots of the polynomial.

Content:
As with the quadratic, cubic, and quartic cases, we need to bear the following important points in mind when counting the roots of a polynomial:

Content:
- If a root has multiplicity [MATH: m,] we count that root [MATH: m] times.
- We also include any imaginary or complex roots.

Content:
And remember, complex roots always come in complex conjugate pairs.
